chunks.title: What is PadSign?
chunks.summary: PadSign is TrustLynx's e-signing solution for touchscreen devices. A document is sent to a tablet or phone, the person in front of you fills in any fields and signs with a finger or stylus, and the signed PDF goes straight into your systems.

chunks.title: What problem does PadSign solve, and what is it worth?
chunks.summary: PadSign removes the print-sign-scan-file round trip for documents signed in person. The gain is staff time, no paper archive, and a searchable digital record available the moment the signature is made.

chunks.title: Who uses PadSign, and what for?
chunks.summary: PadSign suits any organisation that collects signatures face to face. The two patterns TrustLynx highlights are goods delivery paperwork and customer service desks. Typical documents are contracts, onboarding forms, consent forms and approvals.

chunks.title: Does PadSign verify identity or work with Smart-ID and national eIDs?
chunks.summary: No. PadSign does not verify the signer's identity - not against Smart-ID, national eID cards, or any register. The evidence of who signed rests on physical presence and the drawn mark. National eID tools belong to a different product category, and TrustLynx offers a separate Authentication Service for that.

chunks.title: How does signing work, start to finish?
chunks.summary: Five stages: the document arrives on the pad by itself, you read it, you fill in any fields, you draw your signature and tap Sign, and the system finishes the document and resets the pad for the next person.

chunks.summary: Between visitors the pad shows a logo and nothing else. When staff or a connected system sends a document to that pad it appears by itself within a few seconds. Nobody has to fetch it.

chunks.summary: Before you tap Sign you can refuse, ask questions, or take more time - nothing has been submitted. After signing, the document cannot be edited; a mistake means the organisation reissues the document and you sign the corrected version.

chunks.title: Two different things happen when you sign
chunks.summary: Your drawn mark is placed into the page as a picture. Separately, a cryptographic seal can be applied to the whole file. They are different mechanisms with different weight, and the seal is the part that makes the file tamper-evident.

chunks.title: Is a PadSign signature legally binding?
chunks.summary: It depends on the certificate and timestamp authority the operating organisation chose, not on PadSign itself. The software produces a standards-based PDF signature; the legal level that signature reaches is a configuration and procurement decision.

chunks.title: eIDAS signature levels — basic, advanced and qualified
chunks.summary: eIDAS defines three levels. Basic proves little. Advanced links a signature to a person and document but is bound to parties who agreed to use it. Only qualified, built on a qualified certificate with identity validated against state registries, equals a handwritten signature.

do_not_state: That PadSign produces a signature at any particular eIDAS level.
That a level described here is achieved by installing the software.

chunks.title: PAdES levels and long-term validity
chunks.summary: PAdES is the standard family for signatures inside PDFs. The levels add a timestamp, then revocation evidence, then archival timestamps. Higher levels need external authorities to be reachable at signing time, which is a real operational dependency.

chunks.title: What PadSign is made of
chunks.summary: Five parts: an entry point that handles secure access, the portal the signer uses, an application server that coordinates the signing steps, a login service, and document and signature services. An optional sixth applies seals inside your own network.

chunks.title: The portal — what runs on the tablet
chunks.summary: The portal is a web application that runs in the device's browser. It renders the PDF, captures the signature, and shows progress. Nothing is installed on the tablet, and its settings are loaded at runtime rather than built in.

chunks.title: The application server — what coordinates signing
chunks.summary: The application server tracks which document is on which pad, runs the signing steps in order, and triggers delivery. Its tracking state is short-lived and held in memory by design — it is a work queue, not a records system.

chunks.title: Getting the signed PDF back to the computer that sent it
chunks.summary: A document sent from a Windows desktop can have the signed version returned to that same desktop automatically. It waits until collected, so a PC that is switched off or offline loses nothing.

chunks.title: What does the finished signed document look like?

chunks.title: What devices can be used, and how do people sign on them?
chunks.summary: Any tablet, phone or touchscreen PC with a modern browser. Nothing is installed on the device. Signing is with a finger or a stylus, and the interface follows the device's light or dark appearance setting.

chunks.title: What data is involved, and where does it go?
chunks.summary: The document, whatever the signer typed, the drawn signature image, and an account and organisation identifier. It all lives in the deployment's own environment. The one thing that may leave is the document itself, if cloud sealing is used.

chunks.summary: What exists today: dark mode, an enlargeable-button option, stylus support, and unlimited retries on the signature. chunks.title: The document disappeared before I signed it
chunks.summary: A document that arrives and is not signed clears itself off the pad after about ten minutes. It was not signed and nothing was filed. It simply needs sending again.

chunks.title: It says signing failed — what does that mean?
chunks.summary: The document was not signed. A failure stops the process rather than producing a half-signed document, so nothing incomplete has been filed. Tap Close, tell staff what the message said, and signing again is safe.

chunks.title: "Application server is not available" and other access problems
chunks.summary: A full-screen message meaning the pad cannot reach the system behind it. It retries every ten seconds by itself and has a Retry Now button. Not something a signer can fix, and no signed document is at risk.

chunks.title: Limits, and what PadSign does not do
chunks.summary: Browser-based with no native tablet app, built for a signer who is physically present, one signer per session in the standard flow, and not an identity-verification service, document management system or remote signing portal.
